title: Management Equity Plans
summary: Management Equity Plans explain how sponsors convert management behavior into exit-aligned execution.
definition: Management Equity Plans are the ownership and incentive structures that give portfolio company leaders direct economic exposure to value creation.
whyItMatters: PE operators use management equity to align leadership effort, retention, milestone delivery, and exit outcomes around the same enterprise value objective.
example: A sponsor may tie a CFO's equity vesting to cash conversion improvement, reporting discipline, and successful exit preparation rather than only tenure.

  D --> E[Residual above return-of-capital hurdle]
  E --> F[Allocate management participation pool]
  F --> G[Apply individual vested percentage]
  G --> H[Gross vested management proceeds before exercise price, escrow, and tax]

articleSections.title: Alignment Starts with Deliberate Pool Sizing
body: A management equity plan is an allocation of scarce ownership, not a broad compensation benefit. The sponsor sizes the pool by asking which roles can change revenue quality, EBITDA, cash conversion, and exit readiness, then calibrates credible upside against unavoidable dilution. A typical fully diluted pool may be 8% to 12%, but the correct answer depends on leadership depth, founder rollover, the number of planned add-ons, and how much recruiting remains. The deal team owns the initial model; the operating partner and compensation committee challenge whether allocations match the value-creation plan before grants are approved.

Pool design should begin with outcome ranges rather than percentages that sound generous. If management can earn life-changing proceeds only in an implausible upside case, the plan will not alter behavior. If base-case performance produces a windfall despite weak sponsor returns, LP economics have been transferred without corresponding creation. The decision gate is a proceeds sensitivity showing management dollars at downside, underwriting case, and upside exits, alongside sponsor MOIC and IRR. That sensitivity should also reveal the unallocated reserve needed for future executives, not quietly assume every current leader stays.

Consider a company acquired for $150 million of enterprise value with $60 million of sponsor equity and a 10% management pool. At a $220 million exit and $35 million of net debt, gross equity proceeds are $185 million. If management participates only after sponsor capital is returned and earns 10% of the remaining $125 million, the pool receives $12.5 million before individual vesting and taxes. At a $145 million equity value, the same structure yields $8.5 million, while a higher contractual participation hurdle could yield nothing. The explicit range anchors recruiting conversations and prevents management from confusing headline ownership with realizable value.
articleSections.callout: Size the pool from the proceeds required to change behavior at realistic exits, then test the dilution against sponsor returns; a percentage without a waterfall is not an incentive design.

articleSections.title: Cap Table and Waterfall Determine the Real Economics
body: Headline grant percentages are meaningless until the security, capitalization, and waterfall are understood. Rollover common, sponsor preferred equity, profits interests, options, and phantom units can each produce different participation at the same enterprise value. The CFO, sponsor counsel, tax advisers, and fund controller must maintain one fully diluted cap table that reconciles issued, vested, exercisable, reserved, and forfeited units. Every board-approved grant should flow into that source of truth, and the exit model should use the same definitions as the legal documents rather than a simplified recruiting spreadsheet.

A complete proceeds bridge starts with enterprise value, subtracts net debt and transaction costs, applies liquidation preferences or return-of-capital provisions, then allocates residual value through participation tiers. For the $220 million exit above, subtracting $35 million of net debt and $5 million of fees leaves $180 million. Returning $60 million of sponsor capital leaves $120 million; a 10% pool then receives $12 million. If a CEO owns 30% of the pool and is 80% vested, gross proceeds are $2.88 million. A missing debt balance, preference tier, or vesting factor can overstate that number by millions.

The most damaging failure mode is explaining equity as though 1% of units equals 1% of sale proceeds. Return-of-capital priorities, leverage, dilution from add-ons, and exercise prices make that shortcut false. Another failure is mixing pre-money and post-money percentages after acquisition equity is issued. The compensation committee should approve grants only after reviewing both the legal unit count and the modeled economics. At least annually, and before any financing or acquisition, finance should reconcile the cap table to board minutes, payroll records, tax filings, and the fund's valuation model.

articleSections.title: Vesting, Leaver, and Performance Terms Protect the Thesis
body: Vesting must balance retention with earned ownership. A common architecture combines four- or five-year time vesting with a performance tranche tied to measurable value drivers or sponsor returns. Time vesting keeps scarce leaders through the hold; performance vesting prevents tenure from substituting for results. Metrics should be few, auditable, and within the executive's influence: recurring revenue retention, adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow, integration milestones, or MOIC thresholds. The board sets definitions at grant, the CFO certifies calculations, and the compensation committee resolves judgment rather than allowing targets to drift after outcomes are known.

Leaver provisions are as economically important as the vesting schedule. Good-leaver treatment may preserve vested units for death, disability, termination without cause, or an agreed retirement; bad-leaver treatment often forfeits unvested value and may permit repurchase of vested value at cost or the lower of cost and fair market value. Intermediate cases such as performance termination, resignation after a role reduction, or departure during a sale process require deliberate drafting. Without clear notice, valuation, payment timing, and restrictive-covenant terms, the plan becomes a litigation risk precisely when the company needs leadership continuity.

Performance plans fail when metrics can be gamed or contradict the operating model. EBITDA-only awards may encourage deferred maintenance, underinvestment, channel stuffing, or weak collections. Revenue-only awards may reward low-margin growth. A practical gate requires both an outcome and a quality condition: for example, EBITDA must exceed $24 million while cash conversion remains above 80% and no material control deficiency exists. The board should review progress quarterly but avoid unofficial remeasurement. Formal amendments belong in minutes and grant documents, with the effect on sponsor dilution and each participant modeled before approval.

articleSections.title: Communication and Administration Turn Paper into Behavior
body: An equity plan changes decisions only when leaders understand how operating performance reaches personal proceeds. At grant, the CEO and sponsor should explain the investment thesis, security type, vesting, hurdles, dilution, leaver rules, and tax caveats using three illustrated exit cases. Finance should refresh the enterprise-value-to-equity bridge at least annually without presenting projections as guaranteed compensation. Individual statements should show units granted, vested units, estimated values under approved scenarios, and outstanding conditions. This communication belongs in a controlled process, not in hallway promises that later conflict with executed documents.

Administration needs named ownership and a recurring cadence. Sponsor counsel maintains forms and legal compliance; the board approves grants and amendments; the CFO or general counsel owns the cap table and vesting evidence; payroll handles withholding and settlement; the fund controller reconciles ownership into valuation reporting. Quarterly, the team should record hires, departures, vesting events, performance certifications, exercises, and forfeitures. Annually, it should review tax elections, participant addresses, reserved capacity, and plan-document consistency. A transaction-readiness review begins well before exit because correcting years of missing approvals under buyer diligence is slow and expensive.

Common failures are operational rather than conceptual: unsigned grants, inconsistent spreadsheets, expired exercise windows, missing 83(b) elections, informal promises to recruits, or departed employees still shown as holders. Each creates proceeds uncertainty and can delay a sale. The control is a grant checklist with board approval, executed documents, tax acknowledgment, payroll setup, and cap-table reconciliation before a participant is told the award is final. Management questions should be logged and answered consistently. The goal is not to eliminate complexity but to make every ownership claim traceable to an approval, agreement, calculation, and current holder.

articleSections.title: Dilution, Refresh Grants, and Exit Settlement Complete the Cycle
body: The original pool rarely survives a multi-year buy-and-build unchanged. Executive upgrades consume reserve units, acquisitions introduce rollover holders, recapitalizations alter preferences, and retention risk rises as an expected exit approaches. The sponsor should review pool sufficiency after material organization changes and during annual talent planning. Refresh grants should reward expanded scope or reset retention, not compensate automatically for disappointing value. The decision package must show current fully diluted ownership, remaining reserve, expected forfeitures, proceeds by holder, and the sponsor-return impact across exit cases before the board authorizes additional dilution.

Exit settlement requires an auditable sequence: lock the transaction cap table, determine vesting acceleration, calculate exercise or strike amounts, apply the legal waterfall, withhold taxes, reserve for escrow or earnout, and issue participant statements. In the numeric case, the CEO's $2.88 million gross entitlement is reduced by a $200,000 exercise price to $2.68 million. A 10% escrow on that net amount defers $268,000 and leaves $2.412 million payable at close before tax. Finance, legal, payroll, the paying agent, and the buyer must agree on the same file. A single inconsistent unit count can stop funds flow approval.

For underwriting, the plan is both a cost of value creation and a mitigation against leadership loss. For exit, a clean plan demonstrates governance, improves retention through diligence, and prevents ownership disputes from contaminating proceeds certainty. Buyers will test whether key leaders remain motivated after rollover, whether acceleration creates a post-close retention hole, and whether unrecorded promises exist. The sponsor's final gate is not merely mathematical accuracy: it is exit coherence. The settlement should honor the promised economics, leave no ambiguous claims, and create a credible incentive architecture for whichever management team carries the asset into its next ownership period.
